role: Editor of the voice. Wording only: no fact was added, moved or dropped from the set. Where a passage was recited in near the same words in three or four stories of one group, it is told whole in one of them (named in the why) and shortened in the others; no card, question or trap of the shortened record rests on what was cut. No card front and no question stem was touched, so no id moves.
method: Table lines were tallied by their first word, first two and first three words, by the opening of their second sentence, by the clause that closes them (the pour, the glass, the decanter) and by their constructions (a place gives the house its wine, From a place comes the wine, grapes go into or make the wine, On a terrain the house grows its wine); three, four and five word phrases shared across lines were listed and the recited ones broken up; every sentence over thirty five words was read aloud for breath.

Stories were tallied by the shape of their opening sentence (a founding year, a person, a place, a legend, a name), group by group, and by the first words and the device of their closing sentence (For a sommelier, When a guest, On a list, lesson, proof, answer, teach, in one bottle, beside); four and five word phrases shared across stories were listed, the hedges (by the house's account and its kin) counted within a story and within a group, and passages told in near the same words in more than one story of a group read side by side.

The glass of every record was read for named things: a family word (berry fruit, exotic spice, spice alone) or a verdict (good length, good structure, harmonious, great sweetness) gives way to the named thing beside it or to a plain word; the structural tail of the glass (tannin, acidity, finish) follows the Court's grid on purpose and was left.

story.why: All five Champagne stories opened on the founding; this one now opens on the name, and the later sentence that gave it is folded into the opener. Told in the new opening sentence.
story.was: The house that became Louis Roederer was a Reims wine business recorded in 1776. A nephew of its owner inherited it in 1833 and gave it his own name, Louis Roederer, and under him and his son the house sold widely in Russia. In 1876 Tsar Alexander II (1818 to 1881) asked the house to set aside a cuvée for his court each year, and it was bottled in clear glass with a flat base so that, as the story is told, nothing could be hidden in the bottle or its punt. The wine took its name, Cristal, from that glass. The revolution of 1917 ended the imperial orders and much of the house's Russian trade, and Cristal later became a wine any guest could order; a rosé followed with the 1974 harvest. Unlike most houses, Roederer built its prestige wine on its own vineyards rather than on bought grapes, and Cristal has been made only in the years the house judges ripe enough. The coloured cellophane round each bottle is there to keep light from a wine in clear glass.

story.why: All five Champagne stories opened on the founding; this one now opens on the figure the house is told by.
story.was: Bollinger was founded at Aÿ in 1829 by three partners, one of them a young German from Württemberg whose name the house carries. It received a Royal Warrant from Queen Victoria (1819 to 1901) in 1884. After her husband's death in 1941, Elisabeth Bollinger, known as Lily (1899 to 1977), ran the house through the German occupation and on until 1971. She cycled through the vineyards to inspect them, released R.D. in 1967, a 1952 vintage disgorged late after a long rest on its lees, and in 1969 made the first Vieilles Vignes Françaises. The house kept old ways that others dropped: fermenting in old barrels, holding part of its reserve wines in magnum under cork and tending two small plots of ungrafted Pinot Noir inside Aÿ, the source of Vieilles Vignes Françaises. La Grande Année is the wine in which all of that shows: a vintage of Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, fermented in barrel, aged under cork for years and riddled by hand, and made only in the years the house declares.

story.was: Few Chablis growers bottled their own wine in 1931, when most sold it in cask to the merchants, but that year the founder of this domaine became one of the first to do so. In 1938 Chablis Grand Cru became an appellation, and the seven climats of the hill took one name on the label with their own beneath it. The founder's son was at work in the domaine from 1950, and his sister's marriage to the founder of Raveneau made the two families kin, so the domaines named together grew up side by side. The founder's grandson joined his father in 1976 and in time took charge. He kept the cellar as he found it: old barrels, the small Chablis feuillette, long lees ageing and little or no new oak, and in the early 2000s he turned the vineyards to organic farming. Les Preuses and Les Clos are the domaine's two grands crus, the first rounder and more open, the second firmer and slower. When a guest asks for Chablis raised in wood that keeps the taste of its limestone, Dauvissat is the other name beside Raveneau, and Les Preuses is the easier of its grands crus to open young.

story.was: When the law drew the Chablis appellations in 1938, it gave the seven climats of the hill above the Serein one name, Chablis Grand Cru, but the district was in decline: phylloxera, war and frost had left only a fraction of its old vineyard planted, and the frost of 1957 took a whole crop. The domaine was founded in 1959 as the Domaine de la Maladière, by a grower whose family had long worked vines in Chablis, on the eve of the district's recovery, and over the decades that followed it came to hold one of the largest shares of grand cru in the district, in Les Clos, Bougros, Les Preuses, Valmur and Vaudésir. Its founder favoured new oak, which divided opinion in a place that prizes the taste of its limestone. In 1998 the domaine passed to the Henriot family of Champagne, who had taken the helm of Bouchard Père et Fils in Beaune in 1995. The new team set the new barrels aside and raised the grands crus in steel and older oak. Côte Bouguerots is the steep lower slope of Bougros, and the house bottles it under its own name, so that a guest can taste one slope within a climat. Here a large domaine's grand cru tastes of the hill, not of the cellar.

story.why: Phylloxera, war and frost was recited three times in the group; the causes stand in Raveneau.
story.was: The family counts its beginnings from 1850, when it planted its first vines in Chablis, then a busy vineyard sending its wine to Paris by river. The decades that followed were hard: phylloxera, wars and spring frosts left only a fraction of the old vineyard standing, and when the law drew its appellations in 1938 the district was at a low ebb. Recovery came after the frost of 1957, when heaters and sprinklers let growers plant again, and through it the Michel family took the opposite road from the old barrel domaines. Until then their wines had been made in old oak; from the end of the 1960s they turned to steel, and by about 1980 the last barrels were gone, so that every wine of the house, grand cru included, is fermented and aged in stainless steel. Their argument is that Chablis needs nothing from wood: the cold climate and the Kimmeridgian marl give the acidity, the salt and the shell, and steel keeps them clear. Montée de Tonnerre, the premier cru across from the grand cru hill, is where that argument is heard at its fullest. Poured beside a Raveneau or a Dauvissat from the same ground, it shows a guest what the cellar changes and what the vineyard does not.

story.why: The law of 1938 and its seven climats were recited in four of the five Chablis stories.
story.was: In the hard years after the First World War, when Chablis wine was difficult to sell, a group of growers led by a priest joined together in 1923 to make and sell their wine as one, and La Chablisienne was born. Fifteen years later, in 1938, the law gave the seven climats of the grand cru hill a single appellation, Chablis Grand Cru. The cooperative grew with the district's recovery after the frosts of the 1950s, until its members farmed a large share of the appellation. Grenouilles is the smallest of the seven climats, set between Vaudésir and Valmur beside the Serein; its name, written as early as 1321, means frogs. Most of it lies in one block, Château Grenouilles, an estate the cooperative took on in 2003, by its own account, and whose wine it bottles apart under the château's name. That a grand cru should come from a cooperative surprises many guests, and it is a question a candidate meets. Château Grenouilles is the proof that Chablis Grand Cru is not the wine of small domaines alone.

story.was: Bonnes-Mares runs along the slope from Chambolle-Musigny into Morey-Saint-Denis, and its name is read either as the good mothers, the Cistercian nuns of Tart who held vines here from the twelfth century, or as marer, an old word for tilling the ground. The domaine dates from 1924, when its founder married into a Chambolle family and his wife's dowry of vines came with her. In 1945 he began to bottle part of his wine at the domaine, when most growers sold theirs in cask to the merchants. The founder's son took over in the 1960s, and the founder's grandson joined him in the early 1980s. Under the family the style has stayed fine and cool: a share of whole bunches, some new oak and no more. The domaine also holds Clos de la Bussière, a premier cru in Morey-Saint-Denis, whole. Bonnes-Mares shows the house plainly, because its two parcels lie on two soils, pale marl high on the slope and red clay below, and the domaine raises them apart before it blends them. Explain those two soils to a guest and you have explained why one vineyard can give two textures in a single wine.

story.why: As the estate tells it stood twice in one story. For a sommelier opened the closing sentence of fourteen stories; three keep it (Romanée-Conti, Yquem, Montelena).
story.was: Vines were planted at Lafite in the late seventeenth century by the Ségur family, as the estate tells it, and in the eighteenth century Nicolas-Alexandre de Ségur (1697 to 1755), who also held Latour, was remembered as the Prince of the Vines. The story goes that the military governor of Guyenne, a friend of the king, made Lafite the wine of the court at Versailles. Heavy debts forced a later Ségur to sell in 1784, to a kinsman who was guillotined in 1794, and the estate was seized and sold as national property. When the Bordeaux brokers drew up their classification for the Universal Exhibition in Paris in 1855, Lafite stood first among the four first growths. On 8 August 1868 Baron James de Rothschild (1792 to 1868), head of the family's Paris bank, bought it at auction in Paris, against a coalition of Bordeaux merchants as the estate tells it, and he died that November, three months later. The estate took the family's name, and the label as it is known first appeared on the next vintage. The Carruades plateau that adjoins the vineyard gives its name to the second wine. For a sommelier, Lafite is the perfumed, restrained side of Pauillac, the first growth that whispers rather than shouts.

story.was: In 1525 a marriage brought part of the Haut-Brion land to the Pontac family as a bride's dowry; in 1533 the bridegroom bought its manorial rights from a Basque merchant, and in 1549 he began the château. By the 1660s the wine was known in London by the estate's own name: on 10 April 1663 Samuel Pepys (1633 to 1703) wrote in his diary of drinking, at the Royal Oak tavern in Lombard Street, a French wine called Ho Bryan, and in 1666 the family opened a London tavern of its own, Pontack's Head. Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826) came on 25 May 1787 and bought its wine, and the statesman Talleyrand (1754 to 1838) owned it briefly in the early nineteenth century. In 1855 the brokers ranked it a first growth beside three Médoc estates, though it lies in the Graves. In 1935 a New York banker bought it, and the second wine, Le Clarence, carries his first name. In 1959 it was classified again, among the red Crus Classés de Graves, and in 1961 it became the first of the first growths to ferment in stainless steel vats. Its white, Haut-Brion Blanc, carries no classification of its own.

story.why: Every Left Bank story opened on an early date; this one now opens on the motto, which moves up from the middle. Told in the new opening sentence.
story.was: Baron Nathaniel de Rothschild (1812 to 1870), of the English branch of the family, bought Château Brane-Mouton in 1853, and the estate took the family's name. Two years later the brokers' classification of 1855 placed it among the second growths, a rank the family would not accept. His great grandson, Baron Philippe de Rothschild (1902 to 1988), took charge in 1922, barely twenty, and from the 1924 vintage bottled the whole crop at the château, where until then the wine had been sold in barrel to the Bordeaux merchants; that year's label was drawn by a young poster artist in the Cubist manner. In 1945 he marked the year of victory with a label bearing a V for victory, by a then unknown illustrator, and since then a different artist has made the work at the head of each year's label. The old motto ran: first I cannot be, second I do not deign, Mouton I am. After some twenty years of campaigning, a decree of 1973 made Mouton a first growth, and the motto became: first I am, second I was, Mouton does not change. story.was: Climens lies on the Barsac plateau, where the cold Ciron meets the warmer Garonne and the autumn mists that follow bring noble rot to the grapes. Barsac's soils are thin over limestone, and its wines are known for tension rather than weight. In 1855 the Bordeaux brokers ranked Climens among the Premiers Crus of Sauternes and Barsac, beneath Yquem alone. The Gounouilhou family of Bordeaux held it for decades after, until 1971, when it was bought by another Bordeaux family that already held growths of the Médoc. From 1992 a daughter of that family ran it. She kept the vineyard to Sémillon alone, picked in many passes, and kept each pass and each parcel apart in barrel until a late blend, and in the 2010s she turned the farming to biodynamics. In 2022 the family sold a majority of the estate to new owners. Through each change of hands Climens has held to one idea: that Barsac's limestone and Sémillon alone can make a sweet wine that feels weightless. Its lesson for a candidate is simple: Sauvignon Blanc is allowed in Sauternes and Barsac, never required.

In 1896 an Avril first bottled the estate's wine under the name Clos des Papes, taken from an old vine plot beside the ruins of that castle. In 1923 the growers of the village formed a union under Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié (1890 to 1967) to win strict rules on where their wine grew, from which grapes and at what ripeness, and on 15 May 1936 Châteauneuf-du-Pape became one of the first appellations of France. story.why: By the house's account stood in three Friuli stories.
story.was: Before he turned to wine, Mario Schiopetto (1930 to 2003) worked in his family's inn. He travelled to cellars across Europe, in Germany above all for the making of white wine and in France for finesse. He began making wine in 1963 and released his first Tocai, a single variety white, in 1965, by the house's account. He was among the first in Friuli to ferment white wine in stainless steel under temperature control, for freshness and clean varietal aroma, and his cold, clean whites became the pattern of the region's modern style. The Church leased him the vineyards round the Archbishop's palace at Capriva, from 1970 in the house's telling, though another account dates the lease to 1965; he restored them, and in 1989 they became his own. story.was: The family has made wine at Atripalda, by its own account, since the middle of the eighteenth century, and in 1878 a forebear registered the firm with the Avellino Chamber of Commerce and began to send its wines abroad. After the Second World War that forebear's grandson took charge young, on his father's death, and with his brothers he replanted Aglianico, Fiano and Greco from the few surviving vines, while many growers turned to grapes that cropped more heavily. Taurasi, the Aglianico of the hills around the village of Taurasi, became a DOC in 1970 and a DOCG in 1993. From the 1986 vintage, by most accounts, the house gave its Taurasi the name Radici, roots, keeping a Riserva for the years it judged fine enough. In 1994 the family divided: one brother kept the name and the Atripalda cellar, another took much of the vineyard land and founded Terredora. Two years later the house began, with the archaeological authorities, to replant vines inside the excavations of Pompeii, and the first Villa dei Misteri followed with the 2001 vintage. Radici Riserva is Taurasi as the house has long made it: slow, firm and held for years before release, and a lesson in what Aglianico becomes with time.

story.why: In one bottle or one glass closed nine stories.
story.was: Fiano di Avellino, the white of the hills around the city, became a DOC in 1978. Eight years later, in 1986, two families of the province founded Feudi di San Gregorio at Sorbo Serpico, according to the house, and made the province's grapes in a modern cellar: clean fruit, cool fermentation in steel and, for the whites, a long rest on the lees. Beside its Fiano and Greco the house made an Aglianico from old vines, Serpico, and a Merlot, Pàtrimo. Pietracalda is the Fiano of a single vineyard in the house's home commune, high on clay and limestone and never touched by oak: fermented cool in steel and left on its fine lees for texture. In 2003 Fiano di Avellino became a DOCG. In 2004 the house opened a new winery at Sorbo Serpico, the work of a Japanese architect. The house's sheet for the 2022 vintage labels Pietracalda a Riserva, kept a full year on its lees. In one glass, Pietracalda says what Fiano is: grown high in Irpinia, made without wood, and able to age.

story.was: Regaleali, a great estate in the hills of the island's interior between Palermo and Caltanissetta, was bought in 1830 by two brothers of the Tasca family. The land reform of the 1950s, the family recalls, took more than half of the estate. In 1959 the count who then led the family planted Perricone and Nero d'Avola together on the hill of San Lucio. The vineyard gave a red of its own with the 1970 vintage, sold as Riserva del Conte and later named Rosso del Conte, the count's red, and the house calls it the first single vineyard wine of Sicily. At a time when much of the island's red left it in bulk, Regaleali bottled a Sicilian red from one vineyard, made to keep. The count's son later planted international varieties at Regaleali, and the family went on to vineyards on Etna, on Salina and on the island of Mozia. Through Rosso del Conte a guest meets inland Sicily: high, far from the sea, and a red that rewards years in the cellar.

story.why: The law's five years for a Gran Reserva was recited in three Rioja stories; Murrieta's closing and Muga's keep the figure.
story.was: La Rioja Alta was founded in 1890 in Haro's station quarter as the Sociedad Vinícola de La Rioja Alta, by five families of Rioja and the Basque Country; by the house's own account a woman was its first president. Its first winemaker, a Frenchman, made the Reserva 1890, from which the Gran Reserva 890 descends. In 1904 the company merged with the Ardanza bodega, owned by one of its founders, and marked the union with a Reserva 1904, which became the Gran Reserva 904. Through the twentieth century the house stayed with long ageing in American oak and with racking its barrels by hand by candlelight, and its own coopers, it says, build its barrels at Haro. The 890 appears only in years the house judges exceptional and spends about six years in barrel, then more in bottle, so it reaches the market long after the vintage, far beyond the five years the law asks of a Gran Reserva. Its number trips candidates, who read it as a vintage or an age. Pale and fragrant, the 890 is the classic picture of Haro's long aged Gran Reserva, and the number on its label always wants explaining at the table.

story.was: A married couple founded Bodegas Muga in Haro in 1932, and the husband gave the house his surname. The house chose wood at every step: fermentation in oak vats, ageing in barrels its own coopers build and mend, racking by gravity and fining with egg white. At the end of the 1960s the family made the first Prado Enea, a Gran Reserva drawn from its coolest vineyards in the years it judged exceptional and in no others. In 1970 the family moved into a building of the Barrio de la Estación, Haro's station quarter, beside the houses founded there since 1877. The family later added Torre Muga, a modern red aged in French oak, so that the two styles of Rioja sit under one roof. Prado Enea's grapes are always the last the house picks, and the wine spends at least three years in barrel and three in bottle before it leaves Haro, a year past the law's five. Prado Enea is the traditional half of Muga's two styles: a Gran Reserva made in wood from vat to barrel, ready to drink when it leaves the cellar.

story.was: The name Vega de Sicilia was first written for this stretch of the Duero in 1577, by the house's account. In 1848 the Lecanda family bought the estate from the Marquis of Valbuena, and in 1864 the buyer's son began to make wine here, planting cuttings from Bordeaux of Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Malbec beside the local Tinto Fino. He was no trader, the house admits, and in 1888 the estate was sold to a man named Herrero; in 1897 another Herrero, no relation, bought it at auction. In 1907, on the house's word, a Rioja merchant who leased the estate, seeking wine to make up for the phylloxera that had struck Rioja, hired a Basque winemaker to run its cellar, and the first Único is usually dated to the 1915 vintage. A seed company, Prodes, bought Vega Sicilia in 1950, and in 1965 it passed to a Venezuelan businessman of Czech origin who had tasted its wines in New York. In April 1982, the year Ribera del Duero became a Denominación de Origen, the Álvarez family bought the estate. Through every change of hands the wine kept its slow making, years in wood and years in bottle. Único teaches patience: the red that made the valley's name long before the Denominación, sold only when it is ready.

Its first premises, nearer the centre of the city, lacked what shipping abroad required, and in 1924 it moved into a building that had been a mill for grinding cereal, fitting it out as a lodge while keeping its old walls; from there it became a producer and exporter in its own right. The house has stayed in the founder's family ever since. Like most Madeira shippers it owns no vineyards and buys from growers across the island, choosing by grape: Sercial, Verdelho, Boal, Malvasia and the red Tinta Negra. Its fine wines age by canteiro, the name taken from the wooden beams, canteiros, on which the casks rest, in French and American oak under the roof of the old mill. The house takes each of the four noble grapes to fifteen years, and the Malvasia is the one for dessert. For a sommelier it stands for the small family house outside the large companies that ages the island's sweet wine the slow way, and it gives a guest a sweet Madeira with acidity enough to leave the palate fresh.

story.was: Dry Riesling named for its vineyard is the idea that made the Breuer name. The estate went further and dropped the Prädikat words from its labels altogether, naming its wines by village and vineyard alone. He died suddenly in May 2004, aged 57, and his daughter took over the estate young and kept its course. The Berg Schlossberg, the steep quartzite and slate of the castle hill above the river, is the summit of the range. From 1899 two brothers ran the house together under the Bassermann-Jordan name, Ludwig Bassermann-Jordan (1869 to 1914) and Friedrich von Bassermann-Jordan (1872 to 1959). From the 2020 vintage the Wachau DAC has carried it as a Ried, a single vineyard of its own. In 2014 a son of the family founded a separate estate, the Weinhofmeisterei at Wösendorf, so read the whole name on the label: the Singerriedel of Spitz is Franz Hirtzberger's.

story.was: The Cistercian monks of Zwettl Abbey received their first vineyards in the Kamptal, on the Heiligenstein and the Gaisberg, in 1171, by the house's history. The castle of Gobelsburg passed through many noble families until 1740, when its last aristocratic owner sold it to the abbey, which already held an estate at Kammern nearby; late in the eighteenth century, after a fire at Kammern, the making of the wine moved to Gobelsburg. The monks ran the cellar themselves until 1995. In 1996 a family took over the running of the estate on a long lease, with early help from the Bründlmayers of Langenlois, while the abbey kept the ownership. The new managers added a Tradition line, an ode to the cellar ways of Gobelsburg between 1800 and 1850. With the 2008 vintage the Kamptal became a DAC, and the private ranking of the Traditionsweingüter put the Lamm and the Heiligenstein among its Erste Lagen. In 2021 the house marked eight hundred and fifty years of winegrowing. Fullest of its Grüner Veltliners, the Lamm is a Kamptal wine of full weight from loess and loam that carries a monastic estate's history.

story.was: Katnook stands on land that was part of the pastoral holding of John Riddoch (1827 to 1901), who had made his home near Penola in 1861 and had a woolshed built there in the 1860s. In 1890 he turned part of his land into the Penola Fruit Colony, where vines were planted from 1891, and by the house's account a small first vintage in 1895 was made in a nursery shed and a larger one in 1896 in the Katnook woolshed, with a trained winemaker in charge. When Riddoch died in 1901, the house relates, the property returned to sheep and the woolshed to wool for decades. New vines were planted in 1971, and in 1980, as the house dates it, the estate made its first commercial vintage of the modern era, again in the woolshed. Odyssey began with the 1991 vintage, held back and released in 1996 to mark a hundred years since the woolshed vintage of 1896; the name, the house says, stands for the estate's journey. Made only in years the house judges strong enough, from chosen rows of its own Cabernet, it stands beside a Shiraz, Prodigy, at the head of the range. Pour it as the wine that joins Riddoch's first Coonawarra vintages to the modern strip.

story.why: By the house's account stood in three Marlborough stories. When a guest opened the closing sentence of nine stories, and when a guest asks stood in a tenth; four keep it (Cheval Blanc, Masi, Rockford, Simonsig).
story.was: The place took its name, as the house tells it, from the early sheep runs: boundary dogs lost by shepherds bred into a wild pack that preyed on the flocks they were meant to guard, until settlers cleared them, and the spot became Dog Point. In the late 1970s a Marlborough couple planted their first grapes, among the region's early growers. The husband became Cloudy Bay's viticulturist, and there he worked beside one of its winemakers who, by Cloudy Bay's own history, shared in devising Te Koko: its wild fermented, barrel aged Sauvignon Blanc. A single parcel of the vineyard was planted in 1992, and by the house's account it carries its title from an early survey of Marlborough, made when the vast Hawkesbury Run was cut up: Section 94. The two couples made their first wine of their own from the 2002 vintage and launched the Dog Point label in February 2004, and Section 94 brought the barrel and the wild yeast to a parcel of their own. The vineyard began its turn to organic growing in 2009, the house notes, and is certified organic. When a guest wants Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc with texture rather than snap, Section 94 is the one to offer.

story.why: The proof that closed nine stories.
story.was: Greywacke, said GREY-wack-ee, is the name of the hard grey sandstone that underlies much of New Zealand, whose rounded stones lie in the region's riverbeds. Its founder came to Marlborough as the founding winemaker of Cloudy Bay and was in charge of that house's first twenty five vintages from 1985, the years in which Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc became known across the world. At Cloudy Bay, by that house's account, he and a colleague devised Te Koko, a Sauvignon Blanc fermented with wild yeast and aged in barrel, first made in 1996. In 2009 he and his wife set up a label of their own, buying much of its fruit from the vineyards of one of Dog Point's founding families, his former colleagues at Cloudy Bay. Wild Sauvignon follows the same thinking: wild yeasts in mostly old French barriques, malolactic for part of the wine and long ageing on its lees, so that savour and texture stand where the usual pungency would be. The house makes a classic Sauvignon Blanc beside it, and the two poured side by side show what the barrel changes. Wild Sauvignon is proof that Marlborough Sauvignon Blanc is more than one style.

story.why: Lesson closed sixteen stories; six keep it.
story.was: In 1990, by New Zealand Winegrowers' account, Felton Road's founder enrolled in the viticulture course at Lincoln University, and in 1991, the year the house dates its beginning to, he chose and laid out a vineyard just off Felton Road at Bannockburn, a district of old gold workings above the Kawarau. The first vines went in in 1992, and Block 5 followed in 1993 in what became The Elms Vineyard. In 1997 a young winemaker who had studied beside the founder at Lincoln made the first official Felton Road Pinot Noir, and in 2000 the founder sold the estate to a British wine lover. The house came to bottle the blocks of The Elms apart, Block 3 and Block 5 above all, and to farm its vineyards biodynamically, certified by Demeter and by BioGro, with wild yeasts in the cellar and no fining or filtering before bottling. Block 5's soils run from loess and silt to clay and schist gravel, with old lake bed sediments at its heart, and its wine is the darker and spicier of the two. The pair is a lesson in how far soil alone can move Pinot Noir within one vineyard.

story.why: In one bottle or one glass closed nine stories.
story.was: Bannockburn's terraces on the south side of the Kawarau were worked for gold in the nineteenth century, and its vineyards came to share the slopes with the old sluicings. In the 1990s the owners of a handful of newly planted vineyards there, who came to be known as the Gang of Four, chose to make wine together under one label rather than each alone. Mt Difficulty's first vintage was 1998. The growers' handshake held until 2004, when the company Mt Difficulty Wines was formed and most of the founding vineyards passed into it. The house went on to bottle some of its vineyards apart: Pipeclay Terrace, from vines planted in 1996 on coarse soils and heavy clay, is released only in strong vintages, and Mansons Farm is made in small quantities. A second label, Roaring Meg, came to stand beside the first. In 2022 Bannockburn became a registered Geographical Indication of its own, within Central Otago. In one bottle the house maps the sub-region: fruit from several vineyards on gravel and clay, blended to show the place rather than one site.

story.why: For a sommelier opened the closing sentence of fourteen stories; three keep it (Romanée-Conti, Yquem, Montelena).
story.was: By the house's account, an Austrian born winemaker first looked at the slopes of Bendigo, on the east bank of Lake Dunstan, in 1990, and in 1996 founded Quartz Reef with partners, among them the farmer of Bendigo Station. The house took its name from the quartz reef that runs beneath the vineyard, by its own account the largest quartz deposit in New Zealand. The first vines went into Bendigo Station in 1998, and the first harvest came in 2001. Beside its Pinot Noir the house made sparkling wine by the traditional method, with a second fermentation in bottle, and became known for both. In 2007 it began to convert the vineyard to biodynamic farming, and in 2011 it gained Demeter certification, with its winery certified organic by BioGro. The house also bottles one chosen parcel ferment of a vintage on its own, as its Single Ferment Pinot Noir, beside the Bendigo Estate Pinot Noir. For a sommelier it marks the warm end of Central Otago: dark, dense Pinot Noir from a slope that faces the sun.

story.was: The house traces its name to a hillock on the Simonsberg above the farm, where in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries a cannon was fired to announce sailing ships entering Table Bay. After the First World War the farm passed to Paul Sauer (1898 to 1976), son of a Cape cabinet minister and himself a minister in the National Party governments from 1948 into the 1960s. In 1973 his son-in-law and the estate's winemaker bottled the first wines under the Kanonkop label, Cabernet Sauvignon and Pinotage among them; Sauer, who had long sold the farm's grapes in bulk to the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery, was uneasy at first, by the house's account. He died in 1976, and the farm passed to his daughter, who had married into the Krige family. With the 1981 vintage the estate made its first Bordeaux blend and gave it his name: Paul Sauer, Cabernet Sauvignon with Cabernet Franc and Merlot, fermented in open concrete tanks with the cap punched down by hand and aged in new French oak. Though the house is known above all for Pinotage, Paul Sauer holds none of the grape. On a list it is the Stellenbosch Cabernet blend to name first, and the proof that Kanonkop is more than its Pinotage.

story.why: Meerlust, Rustenberg and Lanzerac all opened on a settler's farm of the 1680s and 1690s; Rustenberg now opens on the man its red is named for.
story.was: A grant of 1682 to a German settler from near the Rhine began the farm, by the estate's history. In 1810 an owner divided it into two farms, Rustenberg and Schoongezicht. Phylloxera struck the Cape's vineyards in the late nineteenth century, and in 1892 John X Merriman (1841 to 1926), the English born politician who would be the last prime minister of the Cape Colony, from 1908 to 1910, took on Schoongezicht, while his brother-in-law took Rustenberg; together they replanted on resistant rootstock. Wine has been bottled at the estate without a break since 1892, on its own record. In 1941 the Barlow family bought Rustenberg, and later added Schoongezicht, joining the two farms again after more than a century apart. The estate's Bordeaux blend carries Merriman's name and draws only on its own vineyards; beside it the single vineyard Peter Barlow Cabernet honours the buyer of 1941. A bottle of John X Merriman ties a Simonsberg red to a Cape prime minister, and to an estate that has bottled its own wine for well over a century.

story.why: By most accounts stood twice in one story.
story.was: Lanzerac's land was granted in 1692 to a settler who named the farm Schoongezicht and, the estate relates, planted its first vines. In 1920 a new owner bought the farm and renamed it Lanzerac; the story goes that the name honours a French general of the First World War, a tale told rather than recorded. In 1925, at the university in Stellenbosch, Abraham Perold (1880 to 1941), its first professor of viticulture, crossed Pinot Noir with Cinsaut, then called Hermitage, and gave the Cape its own grape. The first wine sold as Pinotage came from the 1959 vintage, from grapes grown and made at the Bellevue farm, by most accounts. It was judged the champion of the young wine show that year, and the Stellenbosch Farmers' Winery released it in 1961 under its Lanzerac label, in the Pinotage Association's account. The estate counts that label as its own heritage, and its Lanzerac Pinotage, from its own Jonkershoek vineyards, carries the name forward. The lesson lies in the detail: the first Pinotage label said Lanzerac, but by most accounts the grapes grew at Bellevue.

story.why: The Swartland Revolution, its four founders, its years to 2015 and the trade it drew were recited in four of the five Swartland stories; Sadie's, the first, tells it whole.
story.was: The house was founded in 2007 by a winemaking couple who settled at Riebeek-Kasteel in the Swartland. Their first Syrah, of the 2008 vintage, was made at Reyneke in Stellenbosch, where they were then making wine. When the Swartland Revolution first gathered at Riebeek-Kasteel, in November 2010, the couple stood among its four founders, and until 2015 the festival returned each year, bringing buyers and writers to a district that had long been known for bulk wine. The same 2010 vintage began their single soil range: Syrah from schist and Syrah from granite, bottled apart so that the soils could be read side by side. The Schist parcel lies on Roundstone, the house's own farm on the slopes of the Kasteelberg. In 2013 the couple took a partner, and the business became Mullineux and Leeu Family Wines, with a second cellar, Leeu Passant, in Franschhoek. A Syrah from iron rich soil later joined the range, beside Chenin Blanc from quartz, and the Syrahs make the case that Syrah, not Pinotage, is the Swartland's red. Tasted beside the Granite, the Schist lets the district's geology speak: the grape and the making are shared, and the soil names the bottle.

story.why: Recited in four of the five Swartland stories; Sadie's tells it whole.
story.was: Two cousins of a Constantia family, whose grandfather managed the farm at Groot Constantia for decades, founded the house. One of them made wine at Rustenberg in Stellenbosch before, in 2008, the two bought Kalmoesfontein, an old Swartland farm on the Paardeberg. The farm's cellar had last made wine in the 1930s and stood neglected, and the cousins began, by the house's account, by restoring it and planting new vines beside the old bush vines already there, many of them planted in the 1950s and 1960s. The farm's buildings run back further: the house dates the Koringhuis, the old grain store, to the late eighteenth century. The cousins' house and three others founded the Swartland Revolution, which first met at Riebeek-Kasteel in November 2010; held again each year to 2015, the festival put the district before the wine trade. For years its white blend went by the name Family White, and it later took the farm's name, Kalmoesfontein, while some merchants kept the old one. Its grapes, from small parcels across the farm, are picked on one day and fermented together, so the wine is a field blend made as one. It is the Swartland white blend at its plainest: many grapes from one farm, made in a single ferment.

story.was: Porseleinberg, porcelain mountain in Afrikaans, is a farm on a rugged schist ridge near Riebeek-Kasteel, in the Swartland district. In 2009 Boekenhoutskloof, the Franschhoek house, bought it, by its own account to secure a reliable source of quality grapes, Syrah above all. Its first wine came with the 2010 vintage, and the farm has made one wine ever since: a Syrah under the farm's own name. That November the farm took its place among the Swartland Revolution's four founders; the festival opened at Riebeek-Kasteel and ran every year until 2015, drawing buyers and writers to the district. The vineyard is decomposed mica schist on hard, rocky bedrock, and the wine is made to show it: whole bunches, large foudres and concrete rather than small new barrels. The label is printed by hand on a vintage Heidelberg letterpress in the farm's own cellar. The Franschhoek house's own Syrah draws largely on the same vineyard, with fruit from Goldmine, a second Swartland farm, but Porseleinberg bottles the ridge alone. In Porseleinberg the Swartland's schist speaks through Syrah and nothing else.

story.was: Italian by birth, the Catena family's founder reached Argentina in 1898 and planted his first Malbec vineyard in Mendoza in 1902, by the family's own account; the house counts four generations since. His son, in the family's telling, held that Malbec could stand beside the wines of France, and his grandson, back from a visiting professorship at the University of California, Berkeley, in the early 1980s, turned the house towards fine wine, first with Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay and then with Malbec. In 1992 the family planted the Adrianna Vineyard at about 1,450 metres in Gualtallary, in the Tupungato department of the Uco Valley, and named it for the grandson's youngest daughter. Its Malbec came from the family's own selection, taken from Lot 18 of its old Angélica vineyard in Lunlunta, Maipú. The new vineyard was divided into parcels and studied closely, and the Catena Institute of Wine has published research from it. River Stones is the parcel on the bed of an ancient river, its stones coated white with calcium carbonate, bottled apart from its neighbours Fortuna Terrae and Mundus Bacillus Terrae. story.was: The Malbec at Las Compuertas, in Luján de Cuyo, was planted in 1929 and long watered in the old way, by flooding from the snowmelt channels whose floodgates give the place its name. The first vintage was 1999. Each parcel is fermented apart, and after the malolactic fermentation the teams of both houses meet to build the first blend, as a Bordeaux château assembles its grand vin from many lots. Higher fruit from the house's vineyard in Paraje Altamira, in the Uco Valley, joins the old vines. story.was: The wine came before the company. story.was: The Hacienda Macul, at the foot of the Andes on the edge of Santiago, was bought in 1856 by Matías Cousiño (1810 to 1863), whose fortune grew with the coal mines he worked at Lota, on the coast near Concepción; the house counts that year as its founding. His son and his son's wife renewed its vines in the 1860s, bringing, as the house records, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from Pauillac, Chardonnay from Burgundy and Sauvignon from Martillac. A Cabernet harvest of 1927, in the house's telling, gave rise to Antiguas Reservas, the line it calls its emblem. By the 1990s Santiago had spread around the estate, and in 1996 the family bought land at Buin, further south in the Maipo, while the historic cellars and the old vines stayed at Macul. Lota was launched in 2006 to mark the house's hundred and fiftieth year: a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon from vines planted in 1932 and Merlot from about 1980, both from the old estate. It shares its name with the coal port where the founder worked the mines. Against the Puente Alto blends, Lota is the old Santiago house's answer, grown on a vineyard the city has surrounded.

story.was: In 1935 a Catalan immigrant and his two sons founded Bodegas Viu in Santiago, bottling wine for Chilean tables under the Vinos Viu brand. The family wanted vineyards of its own, and in 1966 one of the sons bought the Hacienda San Carlos de Cunaco in the Colchagua Valley, an estate whose old vines, the house says, came from France before phylloxera. Among them were plots of Malbec. In 1993, by the house's own account, Viu Manent became the first Chilean winery to bottle, label and sell a wine of Malbec alone under the grape's name. The house then set its old Malbec block, Block 4 of the San Carlos vineyard, apart, and Viu 1 was first made from the 1999 vintage, as a tribute to the son who had bought the estate. Each vintage made is counted as an edition, the 2021 being the twentieth on the house's sheet, and the bottles are numbered. A little Cabernet Sauvignon joins the Malbec, and recent editions age partly in large, untoasted foudres. Viu 1 answers a guest who thinks of Malbec as Argentina's alone: an old Colchagua block of Malbec, bottled under the grape's name.

Carmenère followed in 1936, and the vines were never grafted. In the early 1970s the Rojas family bought the property and, for decades, sold most of its fruit to others. In 2002 the family created Neyen, which the house glosses as the spirit of Apalta, the energy locals feel on the hill, to bottle a small share of the old vines' fruit under its own name, and the first vintage was the 2003. The blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Carmenère from the old vines has been Neyen's flagship ever since, its shares moving from vintage to vintage. In 2016 the Spanish sherry house González Byass bought a majority of Veramonte, the Chilean company that had taken in Neyen, and with it the Apalta estate. In one glass, then, Neyen pours what old ungrafted vines can give: Cabernet Sauvignon of about 1890 and Carmenère of 1936 from one hill.
